title: What an LLM actually is
question: What is the model really doing when it answers you?
can: Describe an LLM as a next-token predictor, and say what that rules out.
one_line: An LLM does not look up answers or plan sentences ahead of time; it scores every possible next word in its dictionary, rolls a weighted die to pick one, glues that word onto your prompt, and starts over from scratch.

story_spine.surprise: When an AI starts typing a sentence, it has no idea how that sentence is going to end. It calculates a score for every word in its dictionary just to pick the very next piece of text, glues that piece onto the end of your message, and runs the whole machine again from zero.
story_spine.broken: Treating an AI like a search engine that looks up stored paragraphs, or a human brain that plans an argument before speaking. When it gives two different answers to the exact same question, or blurts out a wrong number on word three and spends two paragraphs defending it, people think it is malfunctioning.
story_spine.question: If the machine only picks one word at a time from a ranked list, how does it ever sound smart — and why does changing one dial (temperature) make it write five completely different stories from the exact same two-word start?
story_spine.turn: Once I coded the 40-line loop myself — raw scores into percentages, rolled with a weighted die and glued back onto the prompt — the magic trick disappeared: intelligence is stored in how the machine scores the next word, and committing to a bad first word traps the rest of the answer into defending it.
story_spine.payoff: You can look at any AI behavior and tell right away whether a bug came from the prompt order, the temperature dial, or asking a one-word-at-a-time guesser to plan backwards.
story_spine.honest_limit: This explains how words come out one by one and why answers change, but we are still treating the scoring box as a black box that hands us numbers. In the next checkpoint (Parking Lot · Token Chopper), we open the front door to see how text becomes numbers in the first place.

sections.heading: Explain it like I'm 12: The world's fastest one-word relay game
sections.body_md:
Imagine you are playing a game with a friend who has read every book in the school library. You write two words on a slip of paper: `the server`.

Your friend is only allowed to write **one single word** on the slip and hand it back. They look at `the server`, quickly score every word in the dictionary, write `crashed` at the end, and slide the paper back across the desk.

Now the slip says `the server crashed`. Here is the secret: your friend immediately gets amnesia about *why* they picked `crashed`. For the next word, they pick up the slip (`the server crashed`) from scratch, score the entire dictionary all over again, and write `because`.

How does the game ever end? Inside the dictionary sits a special invisible finish-line word called **`<|eos|>` (End of Sequence)**. At every single tick, `<|eos|>` competes on the scoreboard alongside normal words. The moment the weighted die lands on `<|eos|>`, the relay stops and hands you the finished reply.

That loop — *score every possible next piece of text, pick one, glue it onto the end, repeat until `<|eos|>`* — is **autoregressive next-token prediction**, and it is literally the entire outer loop of every modern **large language model**.
sections.expert_note: Under the hood, modern LLMs don't recompute earlier tokens from scratch on every tick — they cache each past token's Key and Value attention matrices (the KV cache) so generating token #500 only runs a forward pass for token #499 against the cached history. Mathematically, though, the output distribution is identical to re-reading the entire slip.

sections.heading: Why it answers your question instead of continuing it (Pre-Training → Post-Training)
sections.body_md:
Wait — beginners always ask the sharpest follow-up question right here: *'If an LLM is just guessing the next word from internet text, why does it answer `What is the capital of France?` instead of continuing with `2. What is the capital of Spain?` like a quiz worksheet?'*

Because a finished AI assistant goes through **three distinct stages** before its dials are frozen into a read-only file:

1. **Pre-Training (Base Model):** The model reads trillions of tokens of web text, code, and books, nudging billions of internal number dials (**parameters**) to minimize next-token prediction error. A raw *Base Model* really WOULD continue your question with more quiz questions!
2. **Post-Training (SFT + RLHF / RLVR):** Engineers wrap conversations in a structured **chat template** (`<|user|> ... <|assistant|>`) and train the model on curated Q&A examples (**Supervised Fine-Tuning**), followed by **Reinforcement Learning** (human preference feedback or verifiable rewards on math/code) so that the highest-scoring tokens right after `<|assistant|>` are helpful, truthful answers ending with `<|eos|>`.
3. **Inference (Frozen Weights):** When training finishes, those billions of numbers (**weights**) are saved to disk and glued shut. During your chat (**inference**), your prompt passes through the frozen weights without changing a single dial — which is why opening a brand-new chat tomorrow starts with zero memory of you.
sections.expert_note: A 70B-parameter model in BF16 precision is literally ~140 GB of frozen 16-bit floats (or ~35–40 GB in 4-bit quantization). Because weights are immutable at inference time, all 'in-session learning' happens strictly inside the input prompt (in-context learning), never by updating model weights.

sections.heading: Inside the scoreboard: Logits, Softmax, Temperature & Top-P
sections.body_md:
If the weights are frozen, why can the exact same prompt produce five different replies? Because the neural network does not output a word — it outputs a raw scoreboard of **logits** across its entire vocabulary (100,000+ tokens), and a tiny **sampler** turns that scoreboard into a roll of a weighted die.

Trace the exact numbers from our Python lab after `the server` (`crashed: 3.2`, `responded: 2.9`, `timed: 2.4`, `melted: 0.4`, `danced: -1.5`):

1. **Scale by Temperature (`z / T`):** Divide every raw logit by **temperature**. Dividing by `0.2` multiplies every gap by `5×` (`3.2 - 2.9 = 0.3` stretches to `1.5`), making the leader crush the runner-up. Dividing by `1.8` shrinks gaps so underdogs rise.
2. **Numerically Stable Softmax:** Raw logits can be negative (`-1.5`). **Softmax** applies `e^(z_i - max_z)` and divides by the sum so all entries sit in `[0, 1]` and total `100%`. Subtracting `max_z` doesn't change a single percentage, yet prevents `math.exp()` from overflowing to `Infinity` on huge logits.
3. **Watch the shift (`Figure 2`):** At Temp `0.2`, `crashed` grabs **`80.6%`** and `danced` drops to **`0.0%`**. At Temp `1.0`, `crashed` is **`44.2%`** and `responded` is **`32.8%`**. At Temp `1.8`, `danced` climbs to **`2.6%`**.
4. **Trim the crazy tail with Top-P (Nucleus Sampling):** On a real 100,000-word vocabulary, even a `0.001%` tail adds up to bizarre hallucinations at high temperature. **Top-P (`0.90`)** sorts tokens from highest to lowest, keeps only the smallest top group summing to `90%`, deletes the weird tail (`danced` vanishes to `0%`!), and re-normalizes the survivors.
sections.expert_note: Production nuance: even at `temperature = 0.0` (greedy argmax), cloud LLM APIs are NOT 100% bitwise deterministic! GPU floating-point reduction order across dynamic server batches (and Mixture-of-Experts capacity routing) can flip ties between near-equal logits. Treat `temperature = 0` as 'low variance', never as a cryptographic hash.

sections.heading: The Snowball Trap: How forward-only prediction breaks real production prompts
sections.body_md:
Once you truly internalize the one-word conveyor belt, you immediately spot the #1 mistake developers ship in production.

Suppose a team writes a classifier prompt: `'Output YES or NO on line 1, then explain your reasoning on line 2.'`

Imagine the true answer is `NO`, so the scoreboard gives `NO` `75%` and `YES` `25%`. At `temperature = 1.0`, one in four calls rolls the `25%` underdog and emits `YES` on token 1.

Now `YES` is glued onto the slip of paper! On token 2, the model reads `Answer: YES. Explanation:` and asks: *what tokens statistically follow an answer that already declared YES?* Because the conveyor belt has **no backspace key**, it is trapped into rationalizing a wrong verdict.

**The pro fix (Reason-Before-Verdict):** Always put your structured scratchpad or ``reasoning` JSON field *before* the final `verdict` field. By the time the die rolls for `YES` or `NO`, the evidence is already sitting on the prompt slip — and that exact insight is why modern reasoning models (o3, DeepSeek-R1, Claude extended thinking) spend tokens thinking *before* emitting the final answer.
sections.trap_note: Common Trap: Asking for `{ "verdict": "PASS/FAIL", "reason": "..." }` in JSON! JSON keys are generated left-to-right, so putting `verdict` before `reason` forces the model to guess blind before writing a single word of analysis. Flip the schema to `{ "reason": "...", "verdict": "PASS/FAIL" }`.

lab.title: Build the 60-line Autoregressive Loop: Softmax, Temperature, Top-P & Stop Token
lab.goal: See exact softmax probabilities across Temp 0.2/1.0/1.8, watch Top-P (0.90) chop off the weird tail ('danced'), and verify how <|eos|> terminates generation while Temp 0.0 gives 1/5 unique outputs vs Temp 1.0's 5/5 branching runs.
steps: Run `python3 lessons/l0-what-is-an-llm/lab_main.py` (pure Python 3 stdlib, zero installs).
Inspect Step 1 in the output: verify how the exact same logit gap (`crashed: 3.2` vs `responded: 2.9`) shifts from 80.6% vs 18.0% at Temp 0.2 to 44.2% vs 32.8% at Temp 1.0.
Compare Step 2 (5 runs at Temp 0.0 -> 1/5 unique) against Step 3 (5 runs at Temp 1.0 -> 5/5 unique) to see how one early sampled token branches the entire remaining completion.

lab.walkthrough_md:
### `softmax(logits, temperature)`
- **What it does:** Divides every raw logit score by `temperature`, exponentiates with `math.exp`, and normalizes so the dictionary sums to `1.0`.
- **Why it exists:** Raw neural network outputs (`3.2`, `-1.5`) can be negative or add up to anything. You cannot roll a probability die until every entry is between `0` and `1` and sums to `1.0`.

### `generate(prompt, steps, temperature, rng)`
- **What it does:** Runs a `for` loop where each iteration looks up logits for the current tail tokens, converts them to probabilities, samples one token, and appends it with `tokens.append(next_tok)`.
- **Why it exists:** This 7-line loop *is* autoregressive generation. Notice that once `next_tok` is appended, the next iteration cannot undo it — it becomes part of the prompt.

shareable.the_turn: I used to treat AI hallucinations like mysterious short-circuits in a super-brain; writing the 40-line next-word loop showed me how often humans do the exact same thing — blurt out a first word and spend five minutes rationalizing it.
x_thread: 1/ When an AI starts typing a sentence, it has no idea how that sentence is going to end. It scores every word in its dictionary just to pick the very next piece of text, glues that piece onto your prompt, and starts over from scratch.
2/ To clear the Entrance Security Gate of my AI Engineering University, I wrote the core LLM generation loop in 40 lines of pure Python (zero libraries).
3/ Given the prompt 'the server', the model outputs a raw scoreboard (logits): crashed = 3.2, responded = 2.9, timed = 2.4, melted = 0.4, danced = -1.5.

4/ Before rolling the die, it divides those scores by temperature and runs softmax to get percentages that add up to 100%. Watch what happens to the exact same brain when you turn the temperature dial:

5/ At Temp 0.2: 'crashed' grabs 80.6% of the pie. 'responded' gets 18.0%.
At Temp 1.0: 'crashed' drops to 44.2%, 'responded' rises to 32.8%, 'timed' gets 19.9%.

6/ When I ran the loop 5 times at Temp 0.0, I got 1/5 unique outputs: 'the server crashed because memory ran stopped' every single time.
At Temp 1.0, I got 5/5 unique stories — from a 12ms response to a 30s timeout.

7/ Once you picture this conveyor belt as a 12-year-old relay game, you immediately spot the #1 production prompt bug: asking for a YES/NO verdict on line 1 and the explanation on line 2. If it rolls a 25% 'YES', that 'YES' is now glued onto its prompt. It has to spend the rest of the answer defending its own first roll.
8/ Gate cleared. Next stop on the campus map: the Parking Lot Token Chopper — why the model sees 'strawberry' as 3 numbers and can't count the letter R.
